one_sentence: This document argues that divine providence is structurally isomorphic to a PID control system, with proportional, integral, and derivative modes of correction.
executive_summary: This document establishes a structural isomorphism between control theory (specifically PID feedback control systems) and Christian theology of divine providence. The core claim is that God's governance of human agents follows the same mathematical structure as a closed-loop control system: a setpoint (God's purpose/telos), an error signal (sin/deviation), and a three-mode controller (proportional = conscience/consequences, integral = cumulative sanctification, derivative = prophetic warning/prevenient grace). The mapping resolves the sovereignty-free will paradox by showing that a controller can drive output toward a setpoint without replacing the plant's own dynamics. Key evidence includes 13 independent correspondences, predictions about theological completeness, and falsification conditions. The conclusion is that the PID decomposition is not an engineering invention but a discovery of a universal structure for temporal governance.
short_summary: This document is a structural isomorphism record mapping control theory to divine providence. The core claim is that providence operates as a PID controller with three temporal modes of correction. Key evidence includes 13 independent correspondences between feedback concepts and theological doctrines, plus predictions about theological completeness. This matters because it formalizes the sovereignty-free will debate as a control-theoretic question about loop gain bounds.
